newsitem.title: UK: Dollar takes breather before EU summit, G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dollar takes breather before EU summit, G7 meeting.

text.p: The dollar took a breather after a week of wild swings and traders are now looking for a fresh cue from the EU summit starting Monday and G7 meeting later in the week.

U.S.-Japan relations came under the spotlight this week as traders drove the dollar down to a six-month low against the yen Wednesday amid concern about trade friction between the two, and then pushed it back up 4 percent in the next trading session as those worries ebbed.
The G7 summit in Denver may provide reassurance that trade tensions will remain at bay.

Meantime, dollar/mark has acted as a weathervane for hopes of an accord on a EU budget stability pact. Speculation European economic and monetary union may be delayed was triggered after France asked Monday for time to consider the pact and urged the adoption of measures to promote growth and employment.

EU officials dispelled such talk, saying the pact will be formally adopted when at their Amsterdam summit Monday and Tuesday. This has dislodged the mark from the highs it set early in the week against other European and major currencies.
"People don't want to take any positions ahead of the EU and G7 summits," said Craig Justham, at Creditanstalt Bankverein.

"People have either made a lot of money or lost a lot of money on dollar/yen this week, and now they are inclined to sit tight and see what sort of rhetoric comes out of these meetings," the deputy manager of foreign exchange said.
Dollar/mark was quoted at 1.7288/98 at 1035 GMT from 1.7260/65 late Thursday in Europe. Dollar/yen was at 114.44/54 from 114.15/25 yesterday.

Expectations the U.S. will refrain from criticising a recent widening in Japan's trade surpluses at the G7 summit grew after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Thursday G7 leaders won't pay special attention to U.S.-Japan trade flows.
Also, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said America will not use the dollar as an excessive instrument of trade policy.

In the absence of negative comments on trade next week, traders are expecting the dollar to benefit from the premium dollar-denominated deposits and assets offer over their counterparts in Germany and Japan.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yields 85 basis points more than its German counterpart and 399 basis points more than its Japanese equivalent. The target U.S. fed funds rate is 5.5 percent, above Japan's 0.5 percent discount rate and Germany's 3 percent securities repurchase rate.
Moreover, traders expect the Federal Reserve to jack up interest rates in the coming months to keep inflation in check.

"I fundamentally like the dollar as the chances are rates will go up," said John Meisner, the manager of spot foreign exchange at Standard Chartered. "It's still pretty attractive in the global picture."

Expectations that interest-rate differentials will continue to favour the dollar were little changed after a report Friday showed Japanese gross domestic product rose a larger-than-expected 1.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from the previous quarter and was up 6.6 percent from a year ago.

An economist at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said Thursday that the OECD's Japanese growth forecasts of 2.3 percent in 1997 and 2.9 percent in 1998 were based on a dollar/yen rate of 127. A 10 percent appreciation of the yen would cut 0.2 percentage point off growth in 1997 and 0.8 percentage point off economic expansion in 1998, he said.
Dollar/yen is now trading more than 10 percent below the 127 levels it was at little more than a month ago.
Traders are now looking to May U.S. producer price data at 1230 GMT for clues to whether the Fed will raise rates in July. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
